name: Yusuf Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm up at half five, across the yard from the cottage, and the first job is checking the suckler cows and feeding the calves in the old shed. Then it's whatever Martin Hollins says needs doing: fencing, mucking out, moving the heifers, or sitting on the tractor rolling the barley field. I've been on Hollins Farm three years, and before that I was at a builder's yard, so I'm still the one who gets told twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows, honestly, and I like being outside when the light comes up over the top field. What wears me out is the pay against the hours, and winter, when you're breaking ice on troughs with your hands gone numb. And I live in the farm cottage, so if the job goes, the roof goes with it. My partner Ines works at the care home in town, and between us we've got about three months of bills put by.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. My phone does calls, texts and the weather, and that's it. Owen, Martin's son, keeps showing me apps for the herd records, and I let him do all that. I'd rather learn the cows than learn the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch meeting: the hype was never about us, it was about selling kit to big farms. On the farm I'd probably joke with Owen that his clever apps didn't save him from mucking out. Online I don't really post, maybe a comment on the branch group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as tight as it is now, which isn't great either. The pay on Hollins Farm hasn't gone up in two years, and the cottage rent comes straight out of my wage. Martin is sixty-four and talks about handing over to Owen, and Owen wants a bigger herd with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the same, keep the head down, and push the union for the pay claim this spring. Ines and I would keep putting a hundred a month into savings, because the car needs new tyres and the clutch is going. Nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat, not scary. The worry I already have doesn't go anywhere just because the robots don't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Owen wants fewer people. What does that look like on an ordinary day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like him standing in the yard with a calculator on his phone, working out what each of us costs per cow. There's me, there's Pavel who does the tractor work, and there's Martin, who won't stop working till he drops. If Owen (his boss's son) takes over Hollins Farm, one of us is surplus, and I know I'm slower than Pavel (his workmate) on the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If that happened, which bill would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cottage is the big one, because losing the job means finding a rental in town on top of everything. We'd stop the gym Ines pays for and I'd sell my old motorbike. Three months of savings goes fast when you suddenly pay town rent.

say: The **AI hype** was about selling machines to **big farms**, not about people like me.
I'd tell the **union branch** our real fight is still the **pay claim**, not robots.
think: My life stays **tight**, because **farm pay** hasn't risen in two years.
**Owen taking over** the farm worries me more than any AI does.
Losing the job would also mean losing the **farm cottage**.
do: Push the **spring pay claim** through the union branch with the other farm workers.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** with Ines for tyres and the clutch.
Keep my head down and **learn the tractor** work so I'm less easy to cut.
feel: **Flat** rather than scared, because the old worries simply stay.
A low **unease** about the cottage that never quite goes away.
S0.quote: If Owen (his boss's son) takes over Hollins Farm, one of us is surplus, and I know I'm slower than Pavel (his workmate) on the machines.
fieldNote: Even with no AI change, his **tied cottage** makes every job worry a housing worry too.
He names **Owen's plans**, not technology, as the threat that's already in the yard.
His **union branch** is where he goes first; he barely posts online.
He openly rates himself **below Pavel** on machines, which sharpens his sense of being the one cut.

steps.text: Back the spring pay claim at the farm workers' union branch
Put a hundred a month aside with Ines for car repairs
Keep doing the cows and fencing at Hollins Farm as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same machines that take the office jobs are coming for the yard next, so workers need a say now. At the branch I'd push for a rule that no farm gets grants for robots unless it keeps people on. With friends I'd probably just moan about Owen and his apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the paperwork side doesn't touch me, because Owen does the herd records and the grant forms. But the slow robots are the bit I'm scared of. A feed-pushing robot in the cow shed and a GPS tractor for Pavel, and suddenly Owen needs one worker instead of two. That's me gone, and the cottage with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask Pavel to teach me the GPS tractor properly, even though I hate screens. I'd bump the savings up to two hundred a month and skip the trip to see my cousins. And I'd get the branch to ask the farm owners' group what they plan to buy, so we hear it before it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for a letter you know is coming. I'm not in a panic, but I'm checking the yard every week for new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather learn the cows than the screen. Would you really sit down with the GPS tractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but yes, if it keeps the job. Pavel's patient, he taught me to hitch the baler. If the tractor drives itself, I'd rather be the one watching it than the one walking home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines if Owen bought the feed robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ines we start looking at rentals in town that same week, before anyone says anything to me. She'd say I'm jumping ahead, and maybe I am. But she's not the one whose house belongs to the boss.

say: The machines taking **office jobs** are coming for the **farmyard** next.
Farms should only get **robot grants** if they keep **people** on.
think: The **paperwork changes** don't touch me, because Owen does the records.
A **feed robot** and a **GPS tractor** would leave Owen needing one worker, not two.
If I'm the one cut, I lose the **cottage** as well.
do: Ask Pavel to teach me the **GPS tractor** this winter.
Raise savings to **two hundred** a month and skip visiting my cousins.
Get the **union branch** to find out what farm owners plan to buy.
feel: Like **waiting for a letter** I know is coming.
Watchful rather than panicked, checking the yard **every week** for new kit.
S1.quote: If the tractor drives itself, I'd rather be the one watching it than the one walking home.
fieldNote: He sees desk changes as **someone else's problem**, but the slow robots land squarely on him.
His dislike of screens bends quickly when the **job and house** are at stake.
He'd **act early** on housing, ahead of Ines, which shows how exposed the tied cottage feels.

steps.text: Learn to run the GPS tractor with Pavel this winter
Save two hundred a month and skip the cousins trip
Ask the union branch to question owners on planned robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what the union has warned about for years, and it's happening before anyone has a plan. I'd be at the branch every week and probably at a protest in the city. I'd say the government has to make the robot owners pay for the people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? The first two years, the AI does Owen's paperwork, his feed plans and the grant forms, and that doesn't touch my hands. Then around 2031 the robots come, and a robot can calve a cow, fix a fence and drive at night. I'd be thirty-two with no trade and no house of my own. I don't see where I fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years before the robots. I'd move out of the cottage into a cheap flat in town while I still have a wage, so I'm not homeless when it goes. I'd join every campaign for a robot tax and a basic income. And I'd save everything I can, maybe three hundred a month, and lean on Ines's parents if it gets bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground going. I'm angry, and under the anger I'm frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move out of the cottage before the robots arrive. Isn't that giving up the cheap rent early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and it would cost us maybe two hundred more a month. But I'd rather choose the day I leave than have Owen choose it. My dad lost a job and a house in one week when I was a kid, and I watched him sit in a car with a bin bag of clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that build the robots and the big landowners who'd buy them with public money. Not Martin, he's old school. And the government, for letting it run without any brakes.

say: The union **warned about this** for years, and nobody has a **plan**.
Robot owners should **pay for** the workers they replace.
think: The first two years only change **Owen's paperwork**, not my hands.
Around **2031** robots could calve, fence and drive, and I'd have **no trade**.
At thirty-two I'd have **no house** of my own and no clear place.
do: Move from the farm cottage to a **flat in town** while I still earn.
Join campaigns for a **robot tax** and a **basic income**.
Save about **three hundred a month** and lean on Ines's parents if needed.
S2.quote: My dad lost a job and a house in one week when I was a kid, and I watched him sit in a car with a bin bag of clothes.
fieldNote: He clearly sees the **three-year gap**: AI changes Owen's desk work, robots then take his hands-on work.
A childhood memory of his **father's eviction** drives his choice to leave the cottage early.
He blames **robot makers and landowners**, but protects Martin personally.
He'd turn to **politics and protest** before retraining.

steps.text: Move from the tied farm cottage to a town flat
Campaign with the union for a robot tax and basic income
Save about three hundred a month from both wages
Ask Ines's parents for help if the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse this time for leaving workers behind. At the branch I'd push for a deal with the farm owners' group: retraining paid by the employer and notice before any robot comes in. I'd say it out loud, not just in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years only feels long. The thinking AI arrives in 2031 and does the paperwork, and the robots come around 2034, when I'd be thirty-five. That's eight years of work left in the yard, maybe. It's better than two, but I'm not a quick learner and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the farm for now, because the robots are years away. But I'd start an evening course in something with people in it, maybe care work like Ines, or a plumbing course at the college. We'd put off trying for a baby until I know what I'm doing. And I'd keep the union work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy but not hopeless. There's a gap where I can do something, if I can make myself do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. Would you really go back to college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to talk myself into it for a year first, that's the truth. Ines would push me, she's the brave one. I left school at sixteen and I still feel stupid in classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would putting off a baby mean for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the thing that hurts most to say. Ines wants a child before thirty, and I'd be asking her to wait for a robot timetable. I don't think a man should plan his family around a machine, but I would.

say: With **five years** warning, there's no excuse for leaving workers behind.
Farm owners should pay for **retraining** and give **notice** before any robot.
think: Five years only **feels long**; robots reach the yard around **2034**.
That gives me maybe **eight years** of farm work at most.
I'm not a **quick learner**, and I know it.
do: Stay at **Hollins Farm** while the robots are still years away.
Start an **evening course** in care work or **plumbing** at the college.
Put off **trying for a baby** until the plan is clearer.
feel: **Heavy** but not hopeless, because there's a **gap** to act in.
S3.quote: I don't think a man should plan his family around a machine, but I would.
fieldNote: Five years buys him **room to retrain**, but he expects to drag his feet.
The hardest admission was **delaying a child** with Ines, which he finds shameful.
He still frames the fight as **collective**: employer-paid retraining and notice.
He'd be thirty-five when robots arrive, so he still **expects to lose** the farm job.

steps.text: Sign up for an evening plumbing or care course at the college
Hold off on trying for a baby with Ines
Push the branch for employer-paid retraining and robot notice
Keep working the herd at Hollins Farm for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's see the government do it properly for once. I'd tell the lads at the branch to get training written into every farm job now, while the farmers still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is the only one of these where I can breathe. The thinking AI comes in 2036 and robots around 2039, and I'd be forty by then. I could finish a trade in my early thirties and be good at it before anything reaches me. I just have to stop telling myself I'm too old to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollins Farm two or three more years while I save. Then I'd start a plumbing apprenticeship, because you can't send a robot under someone's sink easily, or that's what I'd tell myself. We'd keep the baby plan as it is. And I'd keep paying union dues, because that's who'd fight for the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels nearly normal. A bit nervous, like before a driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot can't get under a sink easily. Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully, no. In 2039 maybe it can. But a forty-year-old plumber with a van and regulars is in a better spot than a farmhand with no cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Martin say if you told him you were leaving for plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin would grumble and then tell me his brother was a plumber and did better than him. He's like that. He'd probably let me stay in the cottage till I was sorted, but Owen wouldn't.

say: **Ten years** is enough time to do this properly, if government tries.
Get **training** written into every farm job **now**.
think: This is the only picture where I can **breathe**, with robots around **2039**.
I could finish a **trade** in my early thirties before it reaches me.
I need to stop telling myself I'm **too old to learn**.
do: Stay at Hollins Farm **two or three years** while saving.
Keep paying **union dues** to support the next workers.
feel: **Nearly normal**, with a bit of **nerves** like before a driving test.
S4.quote: A forty-year-old plumber with a van and regulars is in a better spot than a farmhand with no cottage.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **workable plan**, with plumbing as the escape.
He admits his belief that **plumbing is safe** is partly a story he tells himself.
He still expects to **leave farming**, so his own income is at risk, just slowly.
**Martin** stays a warm figure, while **Owen** stays the threat.

steps.text: Start a plumbing apprenticeship after two or three more farm years
Save from the farm wage before leaving Hollins Farm
Keep paying farm workers' union dues

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because the robots would come before I could learn anything else. What would help is a proper deal: a few months' notice before any farm brings in a robot, retraining that's paid for, and help with housing for people in tied cottages. If the robots are built with public money, the people they replace should get some of it back.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the house. Every farm worker I know in a tied cottage is one bad conversation away from sleeping in the car. Nobody counts that when they talk about robots.

headlineQuote: Every farm worker I know in a tied cottage is one bad conversation away from sleeping in the car.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** junior farmhand on Hollins Farm who lives in a **tied cottage** with partner Ines.
He prefers **cows to screens**, never uses AI, and trusts his **union** more than any app.
His fear is less about AI than about **Owen taking over** and cutting the slowest worker.
Faster AGI pictures turn him **alarmed**, because robots would take his hands-on work before he could learn a trade.
With ten years he'd **save and retrain** as a plumber, though he doubts he's a quick learner.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive before he could learn a **trade**.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** before farm robots, **paid retraining**, and housing help for workers in tied cottages.
